A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ICE research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, correctness appendix, and Haskell linear algebra appendix are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 Table 1 reports original UCI classification experiments comparing ICE with SVM, logistic regression, and Fisher's linear discriminant.

after.justification: v2 reports original UCI classification and cross-validation results in Tables 1–2, plus synthetic runtime and upper-bound sensitivity results in Figures 2–3.

M1.justification: v2 Section 3.2 introduces selection of a maximum-margin representative of the optimal hyperplane's equivalence class for out-of-sample prediction. The core ICE enumeration, loss, viability pruning, and Haskell routines in Section 2 and Appendix B remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 replaces Blood transfusion with Voicepath in the UCI evaluation and adds synthetic datasets in dimensions 1–4 for computational experiments. Habermans, Caesarian, Cryotherapy, and Acute inflammations remain; the latter is renamed Inflammations. Cross-validation on these retained datasets changes the protocol rather than dataset coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains SVM, logistic regression, and Fisher's linear discriminant, called LDA in v2. The new cross-validation table uses the same comparator set. Expanded discussion of MIP, branch-and-bound, and other methods does not introduce reported comparisons against ICE.

E3.justification: v2 adds ten-fold cross-validation with separate training and test errors. New timing protocols vary dataset size across dimensions 1–4 with the upper bound disabled, then sweep the bound on synthetic datasets with optimal error approximately 0.1N or 0.2N. These are added evaluation designs; changes to retained experiments' preprocessing or splits are not established.

E4.justification: v2 adds runtime scaling analysis across sample sizes and dimensions in Figure 2, and sensitivity analysis of the existing viability bound in Figure 3. The latter tests how tightening the bound reduces runtime and examines its plateau at loose bounds. Neither analysis appears in v1 or its appendices.

E5.justification: v2 Table 2 introduces mean classification errors and standard deviations across ten cross-validation folds, whereas v1 reports only individual error counts and percentages. This adds uncertainty reporting without introducing independently repeated cross-validation, seed information, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 1 changes Cryotherapy errors from 6 to 4 for ICE and 9 to 4 for logistic regression, Habermans logistic-regression errors from 77 to 73, and Caesarian SVM/logistic-regression errors from 21 to 22. v2 also adds cross-validation, Voicepath, and runtime results while removing Blood transfusion results. Settings are insufficiently documented to interpret the revised counts as verified same-setting gains.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3.3 adds a runtime derivation and revises the worst-case bound from v1's O(N^D) to O(N^(D+1)). Section 1 adds an i.i.d. VC-dimension generalization bound. Appendix A largely retains the correctness argument, while correcting the general-position definition from linear to affine subspaces.

C1.justification: The claimed novelty of a provably exact, fixed-dimensional polynomial-time algorithm remains. However, the stated runtime guarantee changes from O(N^D) to O(N^(D+1)), and the abstract adds claims of optimal out-of-sample accuracy and empirically demonstrated polynomial runtime reductions from upper-bound filtering.

C2.justification: v1 primarily interprets exact training accuracy through interpretability and practical usefulness. v2 adds a VC-bound argument linking exact optimization to generalization, interprets cross-validation as supporting superior test performance, and explains pruning behavior. Section 4.2 newly discusses the SDP memory/runtime tradeoff and why compiler optimization alone cannot overcome scaling limitations.

D1.justification: v1 provides Haskell code and proposes optimized C++ comparisons as future work. v2 explicitly states that its reported experiments use an efficient C++ translation of that code. Appendix B's routines and the existing repository reference remain unchanged; detailed compiler or hardware settings are not supplied.

R1.justification: The brief prior-work discussion expands into Section 4.1, covering surrogate losses, exact clustering and trees, MIP classifiers, and scoring systems. v2 explicitly identifies Nguyen and Sanner's similar polynomial search algorithm while distinguishing its missing correctness proof. The Alexanderson and Wetzel reference disappears, leaving an unresolved citation in Appendix A.

P1.justification: The overall section order, detailed algorithm exposition, and most appendix prose remain intact. Editing expands the abstract and motivation, updates the title and author list, corrects wording, and organizes the expanded experiments and discussion into Sections 3.1–3.3 and 4.1–4.2. Most substantial expansion introduces scientific content rather than rewriting retained exposition.

P2.justification: v1 has one table and no figures. v2 adds a search-tree illustration, runtime scaling plot, two-panel upper-bound sensitivity plot, and cross-validation table. Table 1 is relocated after the algorithm exposition and reformatted with percentages before counts, revised headers, and bold best results.

improvement.justification: v2 replaces the overstated O(N^D) runtime claim with O(N^(D+1)) analysis and supporting timing experiments, addressing a central weakness in v1's efficiency claim. Cross-validation with variability reporting and fuller related-work positioning substantially strengthen validation. The new claim of optimal out-of-sample accuracy exceeds what the bound and Table 2 establish, including ties and substantial fold variability, but the correction and empirical validation provide substantial net gains.
